surveyDefinition.title: Mobile Gaming — consumer survey (North America)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on play frequency, monetization engagement, content motivations, and response to monetization friction.

segments.name: High-Engagement Spenders
segments.description: Play daily or almost daily, across multiple genres, and regularly spend on in-app purchases, battle passes, or subscriptions. They are driven by progression, competition, and social features, and are the most tolerant of monetization as long as it feels fair.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Players
segments.description: Play frequently but are highly reactive to monetization — they avoid pay-to-win mechanics, are driven by free-to-play options and rewarded ads, and will churn or switch games if they feel pressured to spend. They may spend occasionally but only on perceived value.

segments.name: Casual Freemium Users
segments.description: Play occasionally, often in short sessions, and rarely or never spend money. They are driven by casual, low-commitment games and are highly sensitive to ads and battery drain. They are the largest group but the least valuable commercially.

segments.name: Committed Users
segments.description: Play regularly and are deeply invested in specific games or genres, often seeking high-quality graphics, immersive gameplay, and cross-platform play. They are willing to spend but are selective and demand fair monetization and regular content updates.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Mobile Gaming buyers in North America. It asks how people use Mobile Gaming, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in North America who buy or use Mobile Gaming for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Owns a smartphone or tablet; Has played at least one mobile game in the past 3 months; Able to make or influence in-app purchase decisions (or is a parent of a minor who does). Excluded: People who only play pre-installed games and never download new ones; Professional esports players or game developers (unless they also play as consumers); Businesses purchasing games for employee training or team-building.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy and play mobile games, paying directly through in-app purchases, subscriptions, or ads viewed. Individual players decide which games to download and spend money on, making this a pure B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Plays mobile games at least weekly
Engages with in-app purchases, subscriptions, or rewarded ads
Discovers games through app stores, social media, or word of mouth
May play across multiple genres (casual, hyper-casual, mid-core, hardcore)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Mobile Gaming Usage & Context
sections.covers: Establishes who plays, how often, in what contexts, and what drives their play — the foundation for segmenting by engagement and motivation.

sections.label: Monetization Behaviour & Spend
sections.covers: Covers how players engage with in-app purchases, subscriptions, and rewarded ads, and what they typically spend — the key commercial behaviour separating segments.

sections.label: Game & Monetization Requirements
sections.covers: Explores what players demand from games and monetization models, including fairness, content updates, and technical performance — the criteria that drive satisfaction and switching.

sections.label: Satisfaction & Churn Risk
sections.covers: Measures overall satisfaction, pain points, and what would cause players to stop playing or switch games — the outcome that determines retention and lifetime value.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who plays mobile games and how — frequency, contexts, genres, and motivations — which immediately separates casual from committed players. It then moves into monetization behaviour, capturing how players engage with IAPs, subscriptions, and ads, and what they spend, which distinguishes spenders from free players. Next, it explores what players demand from games and monetization models, including fairness and technical performance, revealing the criteria that drive satisfaction and switching. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, and churn triggers…

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on play frequency, monetization engagement, content motivations, and response to monetization friction.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Usage/behavioural combined with price sensitivity — because in mobile gaming, how often and how deeply people play directly drives their willingness to spend and their tolerance for monetization, and the category's core commercial tension is between engagement and monetization friction.

segments.name: High-Engagement Spenders
segments.description: Play daily or almost daily, across multiple genres, and regularly spend on in-app purchases, battle passes, or subscriptions. They are driven by progression, competition, and social features, and are the most tolerant of monetization as long as it feels fair.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the highest frequency and spend, and will be most likely to cite social/multiplayer features and content updates as key drivers.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Players
segments.description: Play frequently but are highly reactive to monetization — they avoid pay-to-win mechanics, are driven by free-to-play options and rewarded ads, and will churn or switch games if they feel pressured to spend. They may spend occasionally but only on perceived value.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report high frustration with pay-to-win and intrusive ads, and will be more likely to switch games due to monetization friction.

segments.name: Casual Freemium Users
segments.description: Play occasionally, often in short sessions, and rarely or never spend money. They are driven by casual, low-commitment games and are highly sensitive to ads and battery drain. They are the largest group but the least valuable commercially.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report low frequency, low spend, and high sensitivity to ads and battery drain, and will be least engaged with social or competitive features.

segments.name: Committed Users
segments.description: Play regularly and are deeply invested in specific games or genres, often seeking high-quality graphics, immersive gameplay, and cross-platform play. They are willing to spend but are selective and demand fair monetization and regular content updates.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report high engagement and moderate-to-high spend, but will be more critical of pay-to-win and more likely to value quality and innovation over price.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question that settles a tie is cp1 (play frequency), because it is the most direct behavioural self-report of overall engagement, which is the primary axis separating the segments.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who plays mobile games and how — frequency, contexts, genres, and motivations — which immediately separates casual from committed players. It then moves into monetization behaviour, capturing how players engage with IAPs, subscriptions, and ads, and what they spend, which distinguishes spenders from free players. Next, it explores what players demand from games and monetization models, including fairness and technical performance, revealing the criteria that drive satisfaction and switching. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, and churn triggers…
storyline_notes: Replaced the generic 'purchase journey' section with a 'Monetization Behaviour & Spend' section because in mobile gaming the purchase is not a discrete product but an ongoing engagement with monetization mechanics.
Added a beat on 'monetization fairness' because pay-to-win and aggressive monetization are the top pain points in the market profile and are central to segment differentiation.
Included 'battery drain' and 'cross-platform play' as beats because they are explicit consumer language and feature requests in the market profile.
The 'genre preferences' beat was added to the consumer_profile section to help distinguish casual from committed players, which is not in the canonical arc but is essential for this category.

The 'discovery' beat was placed in the monetization section rather than a separate acquisition section because game discovery is closely tied to monetization engagement (e.g., ads, app store features).
The satisfaction section focuses on churn risk rather than advocacy because in mobile gaming, retention is the key commercial outcome; advocacy is less relevant.
metadata.classification_reason: Consumers buy and play mobile games, paying directly through in-app purchases, subscriptions, or ads viewed. Individual players decide which games to download and spend money on, making this a pure B2C market.
